name: Civilizing mission
summary: The civilizing mission holds that more advanced societies, above all those of Europe and later the United States, have a duty to rule and uplift less advanced peoples by spreading their education, law, religion, trade and technology. Rule is justified as temporary tutelage for the subjects' improvement, often alongside an explicit hierarchy of races or civilizations. Its two models are assimilation, remaking others in the colonizer's image, and a paternal protection of native society.
scope: The Western imperial doctrine that more advanced societies have a duty to rule and uplift less advanced peoples by spreading their education, law, religion, trade and technology, as the scholarship on it describes it: the French mission civilisatrice with its assimilationist and Saint-Simonian forms (s6, s9), the British 'dual mandate' and its companion paradigms of mise en valeur, assimilation and association (s7), and the liberal case for tutelage of 'savages' and 'barbarians' in Mill's Considerations on Representative Government (s8). Its own text cited here is Ferry's 1884 speech on the duty of superior races (s2). It excludes modern development or humanitarian discourse except where it is explicitly the same project, and carries no domestic programme.
